schools.summary: Ellicott fixes the date from 2 Kings 23:23 (the eighteenth year) and stresses the strict legal timing on the fourteenth of the first month; Keil reads the verse as a superscription over the whole festival account.
Henry exalts the passover as the chief of feasts, typologically joined to the Lord's supper, while noting the people kept it more in compliance with the king than from zeal.
Gill fixes the place — Jerusalem, where alone it might lawfully be held.
Clarke frames the chapter whole: Josiah completes the greatest passover since Solomon.
Ellicott reads 'in their charges' as 'over their wards' (2 Chron 8:14); Keil takes it of the guards or posts and the strengthening by encouraging speech and teaching (cf. 29:5; Neh 2:18).
Gill: the priests set in their offices and proper stations to execute their part.

Keil takes the Levites as teachers of the law (2 Chron 17:8) freed from bearing the ark on the shoulder now the temple gives it rest; Ellicott weighs three views of the command and rejects the 'set your minds on present duties' reading as too artificial.
Clarke and Wesley hold the ark had been removed by the idolatrous kings (Wesley names Amon) to save it from profanation, and is now restored to the holy of holies.
Gill describes the teaching Levites and records an old MS reading 'who prepared for all Israel the holy things.'

debates.question: What does 'put the holy ark in the house' mean?

sides.position: the ark, removed under the idolatrous kings (Manasseh or Amon) or during the temple repair, is now restored to its place
the words rather bid the Levites leave off bearing the ark about and set their minds on present duties
holders: an artificial reading recorded and rejected by Ellicott

themes: the ark no longer a burden

schools.summary: Ellicott makes the verb reflexive ('sanctify yourselves') and finds in the 'writing of David and Solomon' written memorials of worship (cf. 1 Chron 28:19); Keil pairs a Levite division to each lay father-house.
Gill reads it as a call to readiness and diligence according to the law of God.

themes: the writing of David and Solomon

schools.summary: Ellicott pairs a portion of a Levite father-house to every lay father-house, the Levites to slay, skin, and hand the flesh to the people (vv.11-12).
Gill fixes 'the holy place' as the court of the priests.
Wesley reads 'stand' as 'minister,' and notes the king calls the laity 'brethren' lest the Levites despise or grudge to serve them.

themes: Levites stationed to serve the laity

schools.summary: Keil expounds the triple charge — kill, sanctify (by washing before handing the blood), prepare for the laity — as at 30:16; Ellicott reads 'that they may do' as 'so as to do,' the Levites obeying the Mosaic law as they serve.
Gill: kill the passover in the manner, time, place, and for the persons the law required.

themes: according to the law of Moses

schools.summary: Keil: the king gave 30,000 small cattle and 3,000 bullocks of his own substance (cf. 31:3; 32:29) for all present who came without lambs; Ellicott reads 'gave' as presenting a heave-offering (30:24), the bullocks for the peace-offerings and feasting.
Gill: 30,000 lambs or kids, enough to serve 30,000 families.

Keil takes 'his princes' as the princes of the kingdom, distinct from the temple-rulers, and identifies Hilkiah as the high priest (34:9), Zechariah his deputy; Ellicott suspects a number has dropped out and names the rulers of the house of God (31:13).
Gill notes the gift reached poorer priests and Levites whom the king's bounty had missed.
Wesley makes 'his princes' ecclesiastical — the chief of the priests and Levites — giving as need should require.

debates.question: Who were 'his princes' that gave willingly?

sides.position: ecclesiastical princes — the chief of the priests and Levites
the princes of the kingdom (secular lords), distinct from the temple-rulers named afterward

schools.summary: Keil records the six Levite chiefs and their gift of 5,000 small cattle and 500 oxen, leading into the prepared service; Ellicott notes three of the names recur among Hezekiah's Levites (31:12-15), perhaps leading houses rather than persons.
Gill passes over the list with a cross-reference.

themes: old family names from Hezekiah's day

schools.summary: Ellicott reads 'the service was prepared' as the completed preparations (vv.4,16), the priests on their stand (30:16); Keil marks the passage from preparation into action, priests and Levites at their posts per the king's command.
Gill: everything got ready for passover and unleavened bread, for rich and poor alike.

themes: priests and Levites at their posts

schools.summary: Gill, Keil, and Ellicott take the Levites to have slain the victims, the priests sprinkling the blood the Levites handed them (as at 30:17), the exception now become the rule.
Gill: the lambs were killed by the Levites.
Clarke holds the people themselves might slay their own lambs, the Levites flaying and dressing them.

sides.position: the Levites slew the victims on the people's behalf
the people themselves slew their own lambs; the Levites only flayed and dressed them

schools.summary: Keil and Ellicott read 'the burnt offerings' as the fat pieces cut from the paschal victims for the altar (Lev 3:9), called the burnt offering though none was specially appointed, on the rule that 'all the fat is the LORD's' (Lev 3:16).
Wesley takes them for whole lesser cattle set apart as burnt offerings (Lev 1:10), lest they be confounded with the paschal lambs.
Gill leaves both readings open — whole burnt-offering animals, or the fat removed from the victims.

debates.question: What are 'the burnt offerings' that were removed?

sides.position: whole victims designated for burnt-offering, set apart from the paschal lambs
the fat portions cut from the paschal victims to be burnt on the altar

themes: all the fat is the LORD's

schools.summary: Keil distinguishes the lamb roasted with fire (Exod 12:9) from the 'sanctified' oxen boiled in pots and caldrons; Ellicott adds the seven-days' scope (Deut 16:1-8) and the vivid haste of the serving (Gen 41:14) lest the meat grow cold.
Gill: they roasted the passover with fire according to the ordinance.

Keil: the Levites prepared the meal for themselves and the priests, who were busied with the fat upon the altar till night, weighing carefully the terms for the burnt pieces; Ellicott hears the Gospel echo of 'making ready the Passover' (Luke 22:8).
Gill: afterward they made ready the lambs and peace-offering parts that fell to them.

themes: the Levites prepare for the priests

schools.summary: Keil gathers the singers per the command of David, Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun, and the porters kept at the gates; Ellicott reads 'they might not depart' as 'had no need to depart,' the Levites bringing them their portions (1 Chron 25:1-6).
Gill sets the singers in the court of the priests, playing while the sacrifices were offered.

themes: mutual service to keep every post

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the verse as a summary of the account (v.10), 'to offer burnt offerings' being the burning of the fat; Keil takes 'the same day' to embrace the whole festival, as 'day' does the seven days of creation (Gen 2:4), all per the king's command.
Gill: all the service prepared that day, with every sacrifice and for all sorts.

themes: 'the same day' as the whole festival

schools.summary: Keil and Ellicott fix the calendar — the passover on the fourteenth of the first month, the Mazzoth from the fifteenth to the twenty-first — the legal timing that set this feast apart from Hezekiah's.
Gill: kept in its proper time, on the fourteenth of Nisan.

themes: the passover on its lawful day

schools.summary: Ellicott reconciles 'days of Samuel' with the Kings' 'days of the judges' (Samuel the last and greatest, 1 Sam 7:15) and notes the added roll of participants as the chronicler's own; Keil reads the close as a rhetorical enumeration (cf. 2 Kings 23:22; 34:33).
Clarke (with Calmet) makes the king's unmatched liberality the distinguishing mark; Wesley adds the exact legal conformity Hezekiah's passover had lacked.
Gill: kept so exactly, so universally, and with such liberality as none since Samuel.

themes: no passover like it since Samuel

schools.summary: Keil ties the date back to the reckoning at the account's opening, the last word before the reign's tragic end; Ellicott (2 Kings 23:23; 2 Chron 34:8) reads the passover as the fitting culmination of the reformation.

Henry reckons the thirteen years to the king's death and blames Josiah's rash, uncommanded war and his failure to consult the oracles of God, unlike David — yet it was in wrath to a hypocritical nation that he was so infatuated.
Ellicott sets the scene historically: Necho marching on Carchemish against the last king of Assyria (2 Kings 23:29), the chronicler drawing the following details from another source.
Wesley: their hopes of a settled happiness were quickly blasted — men are often mistaken about the designs of providence.
Gill marks the irony: after so thorough a reformation, great prosperity might have been expected.

outliers.note: Uniquely presses Josiah's own blame — the rash, uncommanded war and the failure to enquire of the Lord after being warned — where the others dwell rather on the mystery of providence and the judgment on a wicked people.

schools.summary: Keil renders 'the house of my war' as Necho's hereditary enemy (Judg 11:12); Ellicott prefers 'against the Euphrates is my war,' and holds Necho spoke of his own gods, needing no Jehovah-oracle (cf. the Moabite stone).
Clarke reports the Targum's 'my idol commanded me,' the rabbinical excuse for Josiah's persistence.
Gill notes only that it was Necho who sent to Josiah.

debates.question: In whose name did Necho's warning come?

sides.position: Necho spoke of his own gods; no real oracle from Jehovah need be assumed
the word 'God' stands as a divine claim laid before the king
the Targum makes it Necho's idol — the rabbinic excuse for Josiah

themes: the Targum's idol and the rabbinic excuse

schools.summary: Keil reads 'disguised himself' figuratively — Josiah disfigured himself, acting against his own character and God's will; Ellicott rejects this as wholly unlikely, keeps the literal disguise (like Ahab), and insists the warning of Necho was really divine, as the event proved.
Gill: he would not withdraw his forces and go back.
Wesley: how can we prosper if we do not acknowledge God in our ways?

debates.question: How is 'he disguised himself' to be read?

sides.position: a literal disguise, as Ahab at Ramoth-gilead
a figurative self-disfiguring — he departed from his own character and God's will

holders: Bertheau (as reported by Keil and Ellicott)

schools.summary: Keil records the wound and the king's cry, 'Have me away, for I am sore wounded'; Ellicott hears in the archers' shot the deliberate echo of the deaths of Ahab (18:33) and Saul (1 Chron 10:3), whose very words Josiah repeats.
Gill: though disguised, the king plainly appeared the chief commander, and so was aimed at.

themes: 'have me away, I am sore wounded'

schools.summary: Ellicott faces the divergence from 2 Kings 23:30 ('made him ride dead from Megiddo'): against Thenius he holds it no literary invention but proof that the chronicler had special sources; the 'second chariot' a more comfortable one, the burial among his fathers (2 Kings 21:18).
Clarke takes the 'second chariot' to mean only that they moved Josiah into another, for secrecy or because his own was disabled.
Gill: they carried him dead to Jerusalem and buried him.

debates.question: Did Josiah die at Megiddo or reach Jerusalem alive?

sides.position: the divergence between Chronicles and Kings proves the chronicler's independent sources, not literary alteration
the account of Chronicles is an arbitrary alteration of the older narrative for literary effect

schools.summary: Ellicott takes 'the lamentations' for a lost Book of Dirges extant in the chronicler's day (cf. Jer 22:10; Zech 12:11), quite distinct from canonical Lamentations, whose subject is the Chaldean ruin.
Clarke reports the Targum ascribing the record to Baruch's pen in the book of Lamentations; Wesley reads 'to this day' of a nation that remembered Josiah's death as its first fatal blow.
Gill holds Jeremiah's lament for Josiah now lost, distinct from canonical Lamentations, which respects Zedekiah.

debates.question: Is 'the lamentations' the canonical book or a lost collection of dirges?

sides.position: a separate, now-lost Book of Dirges, distinct from canonical Lamentations (which concerns the Chaldean ruin)
the canonical book of Lamentations, written by Baruch from Jeremiah's mouth

themes: canonical Lamentations or a lost book?
Josiah's death the first fatal blow

schools.summary: Ellicott renders 'his goodness' as 'his pious deeds' (32:32) and marks the clause 'according to that written in the law of the LORD' as said of no king besides, the record referred to the annals of 2 Kings 23:28; Keil sets the formula in place.
Gill reads 'his goodness' of Josiah's piety toward God and liberality to the people.

themes: a praise given to no other king

schools.summary: Clarke unfolds the Targum's survey of the reign — the child-king of eight, the reforms from his eighth year to his eighteenth, the purging of Israel and Judah — and notes the great royal annals are lost, only the leading facts preserved in Kings and Chronicles.

themes: the Targum's survey of the reign
